clue.text: The end of Reynard

parts.note: Reynard is the traditional name of the fox in fable, and the end of a fox is its bushy tail, which hunters call by a special name

explanation.walkthrough: 'The end' tempts you to think of the fox's death; it is his rear end, the tail, which British fox-hunting calls the brush.
explanation.definitionFit: In hunting language a fox's bushy tail is its brush, the trophy once given after a hunt.

clue.text: Big Man Kangaroo, odd nag, makes a come-back

parts.note: a boomer is Australian for a large male kangaroo

indicators.note: odd means strange, so the letters of nag are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: An outsize kangaroo and an eccentric horse stage a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: A boomer is an Australian term for a big male kangaroo; 'odd' rearranges NAG into ANG.
explanation.definitionFit: To boomerang is to return to the starting point, like the curved throwing stick that flies back.

clue.text: The house at which to seek such a crust

definitions.text: The house at which to seek such a crust

parts.words: The house at which to seek such a crust
parts.note: the British House of Lords is one of two chambers of Parliament, and the aristocracy is a social crust found there

explanation.walkthrough: The House of Lords is the higher chamber of the British Parliament; the aristocrats who sit in it are the 'upper crust', so the same word names both house and crust.
explanation.definitionFit: The Upper House is the Lords, where the upper crust, Britain's aristocracy, sit.

clue.text: It was cast from the heavens at birth

definitions.text: It was cast from the heavens at birth

parts.words: It was cast from the heavens at birth
parts.note: cast here means drawn up, as an astrologer calculates a chart from the positions of the stars when someone is born

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' suggests something thrown down from the sky; astrologers 'cast' a chart of the stars for the moment of birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Astrologers draw up a birth chart from the positions of the planets at the moment someone was born.

clue.text: You'll never get it with only one shot

definitions.text: You'll never get it with only one shot

parts.words: You'll never get it with only one shot
parts.note: reads like advice about a hard task, but describes a volley of many guns fired together

explanation.surface: A coach warns that success takes more than a single attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One shot' sounds like one try at something; read literally, it is one gunshot, and the thing described needs many at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A fusillade is a rapid volley of many shots, so a single shot can never make one.

clue.text: Establish railway works

parts.note: to found something is to establish it

explanation.surface: A company sets up railway engineering works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' looks like a verb but is a noun: a factory where metal is cast.
explanation.definitionFit: A foundry is a works where metal is melted and cast.

clue.text: Accommodation for Esther, worried about money

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go round the letter for money
worried suggests something shaken and troubled, so the letters of Esther are jumbled

parts.note: L stands for pounds, from Latin librae, the old symbol for British money

explanation.surface: A woman named Esther is anxious about paying for somewhere to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges ESTHER into SHETER, and 'about' wraps it round L, the pound sign, after SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelter is a roof over one's head, a place of lodging or accommodation.

clue.text: Reasonable way to define Batrachian Government ?

definitions.text: Reasonable way to define Batrachian Government ?

parts.words: Reasonable way to define Batrachian Government ?
parts.note: batrachian means froggy; in Aesop's fable the frogs asked for a king and were given a log, so frog rule could be called rule by log

explanation.walkthrough: In Aesop's fable the frogs asked Jupiter for a king and were sent a log, King Log; froggy (batrachian) government is thus rule of the log, and the answer is that word with a suffix, as well as sound reasoning.
explanation.definitionFit: Logic is sound reasoning, and read as log-ic it suggests government by King Log, the frogs' ruler in Aesop's fable.

clue.text: Job — who came after ?

parts.note: reads like a question about the biblical Job's successor, but asks who went after a job, seeking it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' looks like the man in the Bible; it is a vacancy, and 'came after' means pursued it.
explanation.definitionFit: An applicant is someone who applies for a post, going after the job.

clue.text: Vest makes one only a quarter nude anyhow

parts.note: E, east, is one of the four quarters of the compass

indicators.note: anyhow means in any careless order, so the letters of nude are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone wearing only a vest is three-quarters naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vest' looks like a garment but is the verb to invest or endow. E, one compass point, is followed by NUDE scrambled to NDUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To endue someone is to endow or invest them with a quality, and to vest is the same.

clue.text: Favourable, giving one French after too much setback in Italian

indicators.note: the French word for one is placed after the reversed Italian word
set back means the Italian word for too much is written in reverse order

parts.note: troppo is Italian for too much, as the phrase in Italian tells you
une is the French (feminine) word for one

explanation.surface: Someone describes a favourable turn of events in a jumble of French and Italian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Italian' tells you to put 'too much' into Italian, TROPPO; 'setback' turns it into OPPORT, and UNE, French for 'one', comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An opportune moment is a well-timed, advantageous one, a synonym of favourable.

clue.text: In heckling a pedagogue, refused to shut up

indicators.note: in means the letters needed sit inside the run of words heckling a pedagogue

explanation.surface: A heckler keeps barracking a teacher and will not be quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refused to shut up' sounds like talking non-stop; here it means a mouth hanging open, and the word runs across hecklinG A PEDagogue.
explanation.definitionFit: To gape is to stand wide open, so something that gaped would not close.

clue.text: Works for the Navy in a stormy sea

indicators.note: in means the abbreviation for the navy goes inside the rearranged letters of sea
a stormy sea is churned up, so its letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: RN is the abbreviation for the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A sailor serves in the navy on rough waters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stormy' rearranges SEA into EAS, and 'in' puts RN, the Royal Navy, inside it after the E.
explanation.definitionFit: Works is a verb here: someone who works earns a wage for labour.

clue.text: Clueful type?

parts.note: a person full of clues, that is one who gathers clues to solve crimes

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags an invented word: 'clueful' means full of clues, which is the business of a crime investigator.
explanation.definitionFit: A detective collects clues to solve a case, so is the person most concerned with them.

clue.text: True blue admission of Ovid's art

definitions.meaning: a true-blue Conservative might admit to being a Tory, the confession broken into three words
the Roman poet Ovid wrote the Ars Amatoria, a poem on the art of love

explanation.surface: A loyal Conservative confesses a fondness for Ovid's love poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: True blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative Party, whose members are Tories: split the answer as AM A TORY and it is a confession.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid's art was love, and amatory means relating to love or lovemaking, while the split phrase admits Conservative loyalty.

clue.text: Put on something classic and look at the name on the envelope

parts.note: to add is to put something on top of
res is Latin, a classical language, for thing
to see is to look at

explanation.surface: Someone puts on a classic outfit and checks who a letter is for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something classic' means a thing in a classical language: RES, Latin for 'thing'. 'Put on' looks like dressing, which tempts DRESS.
explanation.definitionFit: The addressee is the person to whom a letter is sent, named on its envelope.

clue.text: Sing it ? Don't !

definitions.meaning: the chorus repeated after each verse of a song is something you sing again
a command to hold back from doing something

explanation.surface: Someone is told to sing and then immediately told not to.
explanation.definitionFit: A song's recurring chorus is a refrain, and to refrain is to hold back from doing something.

clue.text: Seller of Cockney stairs

parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang stairs are apples and pears, so a seller of them deals in fruit

explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang, from London's East End, calls stairs 'apples and pears', so someone selling Cockney stairs sells fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruiterer is a shopkeeper who sells fruit such as apples and pears.

clue.text: Am insured for repair of the twins' two-wheeler

indicators.note: something sent for repair is taken apart and put together again, so these letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: A cyclist insures the twins' bicycle in case it needs mending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two-wheeler' suggests a bicycle; it is one who wheels two, a nanny pushing the twins in a pram.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanny or nurse who looks after children would push twins out in their pram.

clue.text: Crafty dodges old Bob used to find his divinity

indicators.note: crafty suggests artful trickery, so the letters of dodges are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
bob was slang for a shilling, abbreviated s in pre-decimal money

explanation.surface: A cunning old man uses tricks to discover his god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crafty' turns DODGES into GODDE; a bob was a British shilling before 1971, written S, which goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A goddess is a female deity, one kind of divinity.

clue.text: A phoney intellectual sorts his post

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange, so the letters of his post are put in a different order

explanation.surface: A pretentious academic goes through his morning mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorts his post' reads as dealing with letters; 'sorts' rearranges HISPOST.
explanation.definitionFit: A sophist uses clever but false arguments, a pseudo-thinker in the pejorative sense.

clue.text: No latitudinarian line

parts.note: latitudinarian really means broad-minded, but here it means to do with latitude, and the line with no latitude is zero degrees

explanation.walkthrough: 'Latitudinarian' means tolerant in matters of belief, but the clue uses it for latitude: the line at latitude zero.
explanation.definitionFit: The equator is the circle round the Earth at zero degrees of latitude.

clue.text: Deserter in the red — that's irregular

indicators.note: in means the word for a deserter sits inside the name of the Viking

parts.note: Eric the Red was the Viking explorer who settled Greenland
a rat is one who deserts, as rats leave a sinking ship

explanation.surface: A man who has walked out is now in debt, acting unpredictably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the red' looks like being in debt; 'the red' stands for ERIC, from Eric the Red, the Viking, and RAT goes inside after ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Erratic means unpredictable and inconsistent, lacking a regular pattern.

clue.text: Noted youth leader

parts.note: noted means famous, but also playing notes on an instrument, and the leader of youth in the legend led children away with music

explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like 'famous'; it means making musical notes. In the legend of Hamelin the piper played his pipe and led the town's children away.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pied Piper of Hamelin lured the town's children away by playing music on his pipe.

clue.text: Rag-type tiger ?

parts.note: a rag is a ..., and a threat that is all show is called a tiger made of that material

explanation.walkthrough: A 'rag' is slang for a newspaper; something that looks fierce but is powerless is a paper tiger.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper is printed on newsprint, and a paper tiger is a threat that is only for show.

clue.text: Song of Latter-day Sarah

indicators.note: of here means made of, a song formed of the afternoon wrapped around the girl's pet name

parts.note: PM, post meridiem, is the latter part of the day
Sal is a familiar short form of the name Sarah

explanation.surface: A hymn is sung by a modern-day woman called Sarah.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latter-day' looks like 'modern'; read literally it is the later part of the day, PM, which holds SAL, short for Sarah.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalm is a sacred song or hymn, especially one from the biblical Book of Psalms.

clue.text: Left to return East-for' a metaphorical figure

indicators.note: to return means the word for left on a ship is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Departing to head back east becomes a figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' turns PORT, the left side of a ship, into TROP; E for East follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A trope is a figure of speech, such as a metaphor, using words in a non-literal sense.

clue.text: Where prisoners were gathered round the banner

parts.note: O is round in shape
a flag is a banner

explanation.surface: Captives assembled around a flag.
explanation.walkthrough: An Oflag was a German prisoner-of-war camp for officers in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oflag was a German POW camp, holding captured officers during the war.

clue.text: Father's had five hundred off a Turkish VIP

parts.note: pa is father, with the possessive s kept

indicators.note: off means the letter for five hundred is taken away from the word had

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred

explanation.surface: A man's father lost five hundred pounds to an Ottoman dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' removes D, Roman five hundred, from HAD to leave HA, which follows PA'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasha was a high-ranking official or governor in the Ottoman Empire.

clue.text: Where Amelia finds me, unlike the only pebble on the beach

definitions.meaning: inside the name Amelia the letters me sit between A and LIA, that is among other letters

definitions.text: unlike the only pebble on the beach
definitions.meaning: the only pebble on the beach is a phrase for someone thinking they are unique, so the opposite is being one among many

explanation.surface: Amelia comes across someone who is just one of many pebbles on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase means 'among other things'; in AMELIA the letters ME stand between A and LIA. Not being 'the only pebble on the beach' means being one of many.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means among other things, which describes ME set among other letters and a pebble among many.

clue.text: Cure ham — it otherwise causes such complaints

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing complaints of the joints, so it stands for complaints of that kind

indicators.note: otherwise means arranged in another way, so the letters of cure ham and it are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Curing ham, a cook is warned, brings on aches and pains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' rearranges CUREHAMIT. The definition names the kind of complaint: rheumatic ones, aches of the joints and muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheumatic describes painful disorders of the joints and muscles, ailments like rheumatism.

clue.text: Take mickey out of journalist — he was furious !

parts.note: to rag someone is to tease or take the mickey out of them, British slang for mocking
ED is short for editor, a newspaper journalist

explanation.surface: A newspaper man is mocked and loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'take the mickey out of' someone is British slang for teasing them; RAG means the same, and ED, an editor, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To rage is to be violently angry, so someone who raged was furious.
